title: How to interview a parent without making it feel like an interview
alt: A conversation at an ordinary kitchen table
question: What did an ordinary Sunday look like in your house?
description: Begin with one familiar detail, follow the answer, and leave room to return. A practical way to record a parent’s stories without turning the conversation into a performance.
thesis: Begin with a detail your parent can picture, ask one question at a time, and follow the answer instead of a checklist. Agree before recording, and let a short conversation be enough.
example: Imagine bringing out a photograph of the old kitchen. You ask about the house. Your parent answers by pointing to a chipped bowl on the counter. That bowl may be the conversation: who used it, what they made, and why it was always in the same place. You can ask about the house another day.

sections.heading: Choose a doorway, not a whole lifetime
paragraphs: “Tell me your life story” can feel like a request for an important, orderly performance. A specific invitation asks less: “Who sat beside you at this table?” or “What happened after everyone came home?” You are offering a place to begin, not testing how much they remember.

Choose one photograph, object, place, or familiar routine. Ask whether they feel like talking about it. If they would rather begin somewhere else, use their starting point. A prepared question is useful only if it helps the person speak.

sections.heading: A simple rhythm: ask, wait, follow
paragraphs: Ask one question, then leave space. Avoid filling every pause or supplying the answer you expect. If a detail appears—someone’s nickname, the route to work, the smell of lunch—ask about that detail before moving on.

Try “What do you remember noticing?” rather than “You must have been happy.” Ask “Who else was there?” when you need context. If you already know a version of the story, hear this telling before comparing the two. The point is to understand their account, including what feels different now.

sections.heading: Finish while there is still somewhere to return
paragraphs: Agree beforehand whether you are recording and who may hear it. At the end, ask whether anything should remain private or whether they want to add something. Note the date, who was speaking, and any uncertainty about names or years.

Afterwards, save the recording beside the photograph and a few words that will help you find it again. A title such as “Sunday lunch at the small table” may be more useful than “Interview 1.” Keep the original recording; a neat summary cannot carry every pause or turn of phrase.

point: At A Story, we treat the question as an opening. A conversation can become a memory without becoming a finished chapter—and another conversation can change what sits around it.
product: A Story brings guided conversation, original words, photographs, and family contributions into one private archive.
action: See how a memory takes shape
author: A Story editorial

title: What to do with a box of family photographs nobody has labeled
alt: Hands sorting a small group of family photographs
question: What do you know—and what are you guessing?
description: Give each photograph an identity, record what is known and uncertain, and invite relatives to add context without replacing the original account.
thesis: Start with a small group. Give each photograph a stable identifier, capture both sides, and keep confirmed details separate from guesses. Ask people for their recollections before choosing a single label.
example: A photograph might be called “Grandma’s wedding” by one relative and “the cousin’s engagement” by another. Instead of silently choosing the more confident answer, keep both descriptions, name the people who supplied them, and record what could help distinguish the events.

sections.heading: Make the photograph findable first
paragraphs: An enormous sorting project is easy to postpone. Choose one envelope or ten prints. Give each image a simple identifier such as FAMILY-001 and use that same identifier in the image filename and your notes. Capture the reverse too: a pencil name, stamp, or processing date may matter later.

Keep the physical prints in their existing groups while you document them. The envelope or neighboring photograph may provide a clue. A digital copy makes a convenient working reference so several relatives can look without moving the originals around.

sections.heading: Use four kinds of notes
paragraphs: Record what is visible: three people, a porch, a sign, a uniform. Separately record what someone remembers: “I think this was our first apartment.” Add who supplied that recollection and when they shared it.

Then list uncertainties and follow-up questions. “Possibly 1972” is useful information; an invented exact date is not. Your four headings can be Visible, Remembered, Uncertain, and Ask next. This keeps the growing archive readable without making it appear more certain than it is.

sections.heading: Ask about the edges of the frame
paragraphs: “Who is this?” is a sensible first question, but the answer may be “I don’t know.” Try asking where people stood, who took photographs, or what normally happened in that room. A relative may remember the occasion without recognizing every face.

When several people respond, keep their accounts distinct. You can update a working description as evidence improves while preserving the earlier recollections. If someone identifies a place from a building or sign, note that basis. Future family members should be able to tell a remembered detail from a later inference.

point: A photograph does not need a perfect caption before it belongs in an archive. An honest question attached to an image is often more useful than a confident label with no source.
product: In A Story, photographs sit with memories and attributed contributions, giving relatives a place to add the context they recognize.
action: Build a place for the family’s context

title: How to preserve different versions of the same family story
alt: A family spending an afternoon beside a lake
question: What did that day feel like from where you stood?
description: Keep each recollection attributed, distinguish firsthand from inherited stories, and add shared context without forcing everyone into one version.
thesis: Keep each person’s account in their own words, attach their name, and make clear whether they were there or heard the story later. Add shared context without rewriting disagreement into a single authoritative memory.
example: In A Story’s illustrative lake memory, Eleanor remembers fear, Daniel remembers the best day of the summer, and Maya knows the afternoon through family stories. These are different relationships to the same event. A shared record has room for all three.

sections.heading: Separate the event from the experience
paragraphs: A date or location may be checkable. Whether the day felt safe, joyful, or lonely belongs to someone’s experience. Begin by asking what kind of difference you are dealing with. An uncertain year needs a different response from a difference in feeling.

Ask each person for their account before presenting another person’s version. “What do you remember about the walk home?” allows more room than “Your brother says you were upset—was he right?” You are collecting recollections, not inviting a family vote.

sections.heading: Keep attribution close to the words
paragraphs: A quotation loses something important when its speaker is detached. Record the person’s name, their relationship to the event, and when they shared the account. Use plain labels such as “was there” or “heard this from her mother.” A later retelling is still part of family history, but it is a different kind of source.

If you write a summary, say that the accounts differ. For example: “The cousins remember the summer visit differently. One recalls the freedom of the lake; another remembers watching from the shore.” Let readers reach the original accounts from that short introduction.

sections.heading: Resolve a detail without erasing a voice
paragraphs: Sometimes a photograph or letter clarifies a date. Add that evidence and explain the correction. You do not have to remove the earlier recollection to make the current description useful.

Other differences may remain unsettled. Do not force reconciliation as the price of keeping a story. Ask what each person is comfortable sharing, particularly when an account concerns someone else. A private archive still requires care with who can read or contribute.

point: The value of a shared archive is not that it makes everybody agree. It helps the next person see who remembered what, where the accounts meet, and where they remain apart.
product: A Story keeps family contributions attributed beside a memory, rather than silently blending every account into the summary.
author: A Story editorial

title: Questions that reveal ordinary life—not just milestones
alt: Hands preparing lunch in an everyday kitchen
question: Who always sat in the same chair?
description: Use routines, objects, places, and small decisions to open specific family stories. A short set of questions with ways to follow the answers.
thesis: Ask about routines, places, objects, and small decisions. These give a person something concrete to remember and help preserve the texture of daily life alongside births, moves, and other milestones.
example: “What was school like?” may produce a broad answer. “What did you do between the school gate and your front door?” might bring back a shortcut, a shopkeeper, or the friend who always walked slowly. The small route can tell you something the school photograph cannot.

sections.heading: Begin with a routine
paragraphs: Try “What did an ordinary Sunday look like in your house?” Then follow the sequence: who got up first, what happened before lunch, and what signaled the end of the day. A routine gives the conversation a loose structure without asking for a polished story.

Other openings: What did you take to work? Who usually answered the telephone? What could you hear from your bedroom? Choose one question and let it develop. A list of prompts is a set of possible doors, not a target to complete.

sections.heading: Let an object bring people into view
paragraphs: Ask who always sat in a particular chair, who owned the good scissors, or which bowl came out when visitors arrived. Objects can make relationships easier to describe. A chipped cup may lead to a person whose name never appears in the formal family album.

Follow with “Who taught you to use it?” or “What happened when it broke?” Avoid deciding in advance which object should be meaningful. The storyteller may care more about a lunch tin than an heirloom. Keep that choice visible in the story.

sections.heading: Ask what an outsider would miss
paragraphs: Families use names for places that do not appear on a map. Ask “What did everyone call the place that had another official name?” or “What would a visitor have needed someone to explain?” These questions make room for local knowledge.

After the conversation, write down a few terms exactly as they were said. Add an explanation separately if it helps. If a relative remembers a different nickname, keep both with their sources. The purpose is to give future readers a way into the household, not to make it sound more orderly than it was.

point: The everyday does not need to become extraordinary to be worth keeping. What feels too ordinary to record now may be exactly what another generation cannot otherwise know.
product: A Story offers questions across 11 chapters, with room to write your own memories and return to an unfinished subject.
author: A Story editorial

title: What families should decide before recording sensitive stories
alt: A quiet telephone conversation at home
question: What would you like to keep just between us?
description: Agree on recording, access, review, and subjects to leave aside before a sensitive family conversation. Preserve the storyteller’s ability to change course.
thesis: Discuss whether to record, who may hear or read the result, what should remain private, and how the storyteller can review it. Make those decisions before the conversation becomes difficult.
example: A parent is comfortable describing a move but does not want to discuss the family disagreement around it. You can keep the story of the new home without treating that boundary as a missing answer to extract. Another conversation may happen later, or it may not.

sections.heading: Agree on the audience in ordinary language
paragraphs: “For the family” can mean different things to different people. Name the intended readers or listeners. Explain whether the recording will stay with one person, go into a shared archive, or be used in a printed volume.

Ask separately about recording and sharing. Being comfortable speaking to you does not automatically mean being comfortable with a recording or a wider audience. The Oral History Association’s principles place attention on participants’ understanding and involvement throughout the process; see the further-reading link below.

sections.heading: Make stopping easy
paragraphs: Agree on a plain way to pause: “We can leave that there” is enough. Do not require someone to explain or justify a boundary. Offer to move to another topic or stop for the day, and follow the choice they make.

Leave room for a person to change their mind about what they have just said. Discuss how the material will be reviewed before it is shared, and what you can actually remove or restrict in the tools you are using. Do not promise a control you have not checked.

sections.heading: Keep other people in mind
paragraphs: A story can concern people who are not in the room. Before sharing an account, consider whose private information it includes and whether those details are needed for the intended audience. Keeping a recollection does not require making every part of it widely accessible.

Afterwards, confirm what was agreed and keep a note with the material. Ask the storyteller to review any summary that could change the sense of their account. Attribution is essential, but a name beside a quotation does not by itself settle whether it should be shared.

point: An archive earns trust through the choices it respects. A story left untold today is not a failed conversation.
product: A Story is private by default. Families decide whom to invite; a conversation about boundaries should come before any invitation.

source.label: Oral History Association: Principles and Best Practices

author: A Story editorial

title: For care communities: planning participation, consent, and family contribution
alt: People listening and adding context to family photographs
question: How would you like to take part?
description: Plan a resident-led storytelling project around preferences, consent, family contribution, staff involvement, and clear archive access.
thesis: Plan the participation before planning the content. Begin with the resident’s wishes, agree how family and staff will be involved, and define who may access the archive and how those arrangements will be revisited.
example: A resident wants to talk about the shop where she worked. Her daughter can identify the people in a photograph; a staff member can help find a quiet time. These are three different contributions. The resident should not become a supporting character in a project organized around her life.

sections.heading: Write a one-page participation plan
paragraphs: Start with five headings: Preferences, Recording, Family contribution, Staff involvement, and Access. Under each, note what has been agreed and what still needs discussion. Use names and practical arrangements instead of broad promises.

Preferences might include time of day, conversation length, subjects to avoid, and whether another person should be present. Recording and access need their own discussion. The plan should make it easy to see who is responsible for checking that the arrangement still fits the resident’s wishes.

sections.heading: Give family and staff distinct roles
paragraphs: Relatives may contribute photographs, identify names, or add another recollection. Ask them to distinguish what they witnessed from what they heard later. Keep their contribution attributed rather than silently editing it into the resident’s words.

Staff involvement may be as simple as helping coordinate setup or a comfortable space. Do not build a launch plan around tools or staffing capacity that have not been confirmed. A small, workable arrangement is more useful than a long list of proposed features.

sections.heading: Make review part of the project
paragraphs: Before wider sharing, revisit who will be able to see the material and whether that matches what participants understood. Establish how someone can raise a concern or ask to pause participation. Consult the community’s relevant policies and responsible staff for consent and access requirements.

Do not treat a completed form as a substitute for listening to the person during the conversation. If preferences or circumstances change, pause and review the arrangement. The project’s purpose is to make room for a person’s history, not to meet a recording quota.

point: A Story’s starting point for care communities is personhood: the resident’s voice, the family’s context, and a participation plan that makes sense for the people involved.
product: A demonstration is a chance to discuss the scope, participants, and access needs before anything is set up.
action: Explore A Story for care communities

title: How organizations can preserve context before long-serving people retire
alt: A craftsperson working at a repair bench
question: What does the written procedure leave out?
description: Capture the decisions, exceptions, and relationships behind routine work before a long-serving colleague leaves. A practical oral-history framework.
thesis: Choose a few decisions that depend on experience, ask the person to walk through real examples, and keep the reasoning beside the documents it explains. Agree on scope and access before recording.
example: A workshop has a maintenance notebook, but one colleague knows which sound means a job needs a second look. Asking her to read out the procedure will miss that knowledge. Asking about the last time she stopped a job may reveal the judgment a successor needs to understand.

sections.heading: Start with the work someone actually does
paragraphs: List three situations that regularly lead people to ask this colleague for help. They might involve an unusual failure, a long-standing relationship, or a decision that never appears in the standard procedure.

Choose one situation for the first conversation. Ask for a specific occurrence: what they noticed, what they considered, what they did, and what happened next. A concrete example gives later readers a way to understand the reasoning without pretending that one anecdote is a universal rule.

sections.heading: Keep the explanation attached to its context
paragraphs: Pair the account with the relevant photograph, document, place, or period. Record who is speaking and when. If a practice has changed, make that clear rather than allowing an old recollection to look like current operating guidance.

Ask “What would you have done differently if this other condition had been present?” and “Who else understood this problem?” These questions can identify limits and other sources. A useful archive shows where an account applies and where someone should look further.

sections.heading: Invite a second perspective and plan the handover
paragraphs: A colleague may remember the same change from another role. Keep that account alongside the first, with its attribution. A founder’s explanation and a technician’s experience may reveal different parts of the same decision.

Before the person leaves, ask a future reader to try finding and understanding one example. Can they locate it from the words they would naturally search for? Do the documents and recollections refer to the same event? Fix unclear names and missing context while someone can still help.

Agree who may see the material and what must remain restricted. Preserve oral history as context; keep approved procedures, responsibilities, and current instructions in the organization’s appropriate working systems.

point: Institutional memory is more useful when it preserves judgment and context, not just a polished account of success. The hesitation, exception, and second recollection may be the part a future colleague needs.
product: A Story can begin with a clearly scoped organizational history project, using attributed recollections and photographs to keep the people behind the record visible.
author: A Story editorial
